title: A Phone ≠ A Brain
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart responds to the idea that facts retrievable on a smartphone need not be taught. He argues that a person with knowledge in their head has more power and more joy than one who must look everything up, illustrating with his own work on Indian Education for All in Montana and his growing grasp of the Common Core. What changed across his scenarios was that the knowledge in his head grew, strengthened, and cohered, making the work more engaging and less tedious. He concludes that schools should be built on knowledge-rich, coherent, sequenced curricula, that equitable outcomes depend on this, and that teaching only what students will need is an impoverished view of education.
points: Knowledge held in the head gives more power and more joy than knowledge available only on the internet.
Internalized knowledge makes work more relevant and engaging and less tedious.
Stuart's own experience with the Common Core shows knowledge deepening as it moves from reading to writing to distilling.
The 'it's on your phone' argument should be answered by building knowledge-rich, sequenced curricula.
Teaching only what students will 'need' impoverishes education, and equity requires broad knowledge for all.
quotes: Perhaps the day will come when human beings attach their brains to the Internet and become one with the digitized knowledge-base. Billionaires are investing in this kind of research, and the science is fascinating, bizarre, and frightening.
The knowledge in my head will make the work more relevant, more interesting, more engaging. It’ll also be less likely to be tedious, troublesome, and confusing.

What changed in those three scenarios — me hearing and reading about Common Core, me reading the standards themselves and then writing about them, and me reducing the standards into something a mortal can teach? Well, lots of things — not the least of which is that what I knew about the standards in my head (vs in a book or in someone else’s words) grew, strengthened, and cohered.

So even though it is common to theorize that any information retrievable on a smartphone is not information that a student should be given the chance to learn, let’s think harder than this. And enough about what our students need to know — let’s talk about what our students, all of them, will get to know thanks to the knowledge-rich, coherent, and logically-sequenced curricula on which we build our schools.
By the way, woe to us when all we care about teaching our students is what they’ll “need.” This is an impoverished view of education.
